What Is the Stock Market? Meaning, How It Works and Key Terms

The stock market is where shares of listed companies are bought and sold through regulated exchanges. Companies use it to raise money, and investors use it to own part of a business and to trade that ownership.

2 min readFor MBA, BBA and BBMUpdated 2 November 2026

Meaning of the stock market

A share is a small unit of ownership in a company. When a company lists on an exchange, anyone with a demat account can buy or sell its shares through a broker. Prices move with supply and demand, which in turn reflect what buyers and sellers expect of the business and the economy.

Why stock markets exist

  • Companies raise long-term capital without taking on debt.
  • Investors can share in business growth through price rises and dividends.
  • Liquidity lets investors sell whenever they wish, at the market price.
  • Prices give a continuous public view of what a company is worth.

How a trade works in India

  • You place a buy order through your broker's app, using your trading account.
  • The order goes to the exchange, where a computer matches it with a seller's order at a matching price.
  • A clearing corporation guarantees the trade, so you do not depend on the unknown seller.
  • Settlement takes place on a T+1 basis: shares reach your demat account, held at NSDL or CDSL, one working day after the trade.

The main players

PlayerRole
SEBIRegulates the market and protects investors
NSE and BSERun the exchanges where trades take place
BrokersPlace orders for clients
Depositories (NSDL, CDSL)Hold shares electronically
Clearing corporationsSettle trades and guarantee them
Institutional investors (FIIs, DIIs)Invest large pools of money and strongly influence prices
Retail investorsIndividuals investing their own money

Indices: NIFTY 50 and SENSEX

An index tracks a selected basket of shares and summarises how the market is doing. The NIFTY 50 covers 50 large companies on the NSE, and the SENSEX covers 30 on the BSE. Both are free-float weighted, so a company with more shares available for public trading has more influence on the index.

Market capitalisation: a short example

Market cap = share price × number of shares. A company with 10 crore shares at ₹500 has a market cap of ₹5,000 crore. A share priced at ₹500 is not automatically costlier than one at ₹50: price means little without earnings and share count.

SEBI classes the top 100 companies by market cap as large cap, the next 150 as mid cap, and the rest as small cap.

Investing, trading and speculation

Investors buy businesses and hold them for years, focusing on fundamentals. Traders try to profit from shorter price moves, using technical analysis, risk rules and often leverage. Speculation involves taking high risk on a price view with little analysis. SEBI's own studies have found that most individual F&O traders lose money, which is worth remembering.

Risks to understand

  • Market risk: the whole market can fall, however good a single company is.
  • Company risk: management, debt or competition can hurt one business.
  • Liquidity risk: small shares can be hard to sell at a fair price.
  • Behavioural risk: fear and greed push people to buy high and sell low.

Exam and interview questions

What is the stock market in simple words?

A regulated marketplace in which shares of listed companies are bought and sold. Buying a share makes you a part-owner of the company.

What is the difference between a stock exchange and the stock market?

The stock market is the whole system of issuing and trading shares. A stock exchange, such as NSE or BSE, is the specific platform on which trades are matched.

Who regulates the stock market in India?

The Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI), set up as a statutory body under the SEBI Act, 1992.

Does a company get money when its shares are traded?

Only when it issues new shares in the primary market. Trades between investors in the secondary market pass money only from buyer to seller.
